Before you begin

Work in pairs. One person runs the supplied code, the other reads the figure and writes the interpretation. Swap roles during the exercise. Predict before running each comparison. All required code is complete.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and the result sheet locally and answer the same questions. There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled. No installation, independent Stan programming or homework is required.

library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(patchwork)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))
source(here("R/course_utils.R"))
source(here("R/course_visuals.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size=14))

Core exercise: how do data and priors change the answer?

Purpose Explain how the amount of data and the prior affect uncertainty about seedling survival.
Time 12 minutes: 8 minutes prediction, code and pair discussion, then 4 minutes explanation.
Computation Exact Beta updating. No Stan inference or compilation.
Model Survivors y \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(N,p), with p \sim \operatorname{Beta}(a,b).

1. More data, same observed proportion (4 minutes)

We observed 2 survivors out of 5 seedlings. Compare this with 40 out of 100. Keep the observed proportion at 0.4 and the prior at Beta(1,1).

Predict first: which posterior distribution will be narrower?

plot_update(2, 5, 1, 1)
plot_update(40, 100, 1, 1)

Write one sentence describing what changes and what stays the same. The likelihood curves are rescaled to area 1 to make their shapes comparable. They are functions of p with the data held fixed.

2. A different prior, same data (4 minutes)

Keep the data at 2 survivors out of 5. Compare the first plot above with this one. Beta(8,2) gives more prior weight to high survival probabilities.

Predict first: which way will the posterior move?

plot_update(2, 5, 8, 2)

Write one sentence about the change. What ecological evidence could justify this prior for seedlings in the habitat you study?

TipSolution and instructor notes

The first comparison changes only sample size. With the flat prior, the posteriors are Beta(3,4) and Beta(41,61). Both favour survival probabilities near the observed proportion, but the larger data set gives a narrower posterior.

The second comparison changes only the prior. The posterior becomes Beta(10,5), with mean 0.67, instead of 0.43 under the flat prior. Both the data and the prior contribute. The peak need not equal the observed proportion.

A high-survival prior needs support from earlier work in a comparable habitat and census period. The numerical Beta parameters are teaching contrasts, not general recommendations. Check whether participants are describing the entire distribution or just its highest point. A peak is the MAP, not the posterior mean.

Instructor demonstration: Stan reads the same model

This is a demonstration after the core exercise. Follow the mapping from data to unknown survival probability and assumptions. Running these chunks is optional.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;             // number of seedlings
  int<lower=0, upper=N> y;    // number of survivors
  real<lower=0> a;            // prior: p ~ Beta(a, b)
  real<lower=0> b;
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> p;   // survival probability
}

model {
  // prior
  p ~ beta(a, b);
  // likelihood
  y ~ binomial(N, p);
}
fit <- course_fit("day1_seedling")
draws <- fit$draws
fit$source
#> [1] "precomputed"
plot_update(2, 5, 1, 1) +
  geom_histogram(data=as_tibble(draws), aes(x=p, y=after_stat(density)),
                 inherit.aes=FALSE, bins=30, fill="grey40", alpha=.2)

The histogram approximates the exact posterior curve. Stan returns samples from a distribution. It does not return only a best value. The saved result uses the same 2/5 data and Beta(1,1) prior as our first plot.

Optional extension: a numerical summary

Do this after the core exercise or after class. The data and model stay fixed.

draws <- course_fit("day1_seedling")$draws
summarise_update(2, 5, 1, 1)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   data  prior        mle post_mean    q5   q95
#>   <chr> <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2/5   Beta(1, 1)   0.4     0.429 0.153 0.729
mean(draws$p)
#> [1] 0.4251282
quantile(draws$p, c(0.05, 0.95))
#>        5%       95%
#> 0.1505791 0.7226701
mean(draws$p > 0.5)
#> [1] 0.3375

Interpret the interval in words. What does the last line estimate?

TipSolution and instructor notes

The interval describes uncertainty about the survival probability, conditional on the model, prior and data. The final line approximates the posterior probability that p>0.5. Small differences between the exact Beta calculations and saved Stan draws reflect Monte Carlo approximation. These summaries are optional today.

Reflection

What did you learn from the distribution that you could not learn from 2/5 alone? On Day 2 we keep the binomial model and let survival probability depend on density.
